p.x:
Last Sunday, my class went to the zoo in Chiang Mai. We saw many animals from different countries. My favourite was the panda. It was very lazy and just ate bamboo all day!
Next, we visited the bird area. There were parrots with red and green feathers, and a big eagle with huge wings. Then we saw a tiger. It was sleeping, but its long tail moved from side to side. I was a little afraid of the snakes, so I didn't stay there long.
In the afternoon, we watched the elephants. A keeper explained that the zoo staff feed them more than 100 kilograms of food every day. He said that elephants in the wild walk many kilometres to find food. Before we left, our teacher asked, "Which animal did you like best?" Everyone shouted a different answer!

Happy Paws is an animal shelter on the edge of Bangkok. It looks after more than 300 dogs and cats that have been abandoned or rescued from the streets. Many arrive hungry and sick. Some were pets that their owners no longer wanted; others were born on the street and have had to survive alone.
The shelter's staff give the animals medical care, food and, most importantly, a safe place to rest. Dogs that are aggressive at first are kept in separate cages until they learn to trust people again. "Every creature deserves kindness," says the manager, Khun Lek.
The shelter tries to find new homes for the animals. Before anyone can adopt a dog, staff visit their home to make sure it is suitable. They also encourage owners to sterilise their pets, so they don't breed and create more homeless animals. "We can't protect every animal," Khun Lek says, "but we can change the lives of the ones who come here."

For centuries, Asian elephants were domesticated in Thailand and used to carry heavy logs out of the forest. When logging was banned in 1989, thousands of working elephants and their keepers suddenly had no income. Many turned to tourism, offering elephant rides and street shows.
Animal welfare groups argue that life in captivity is hard for such intelligent animals. Elephants are not nocturnal, but in the wild they walk long distances, sometimes migrating seasonally in search of food, and live in close family groups. Their natural instinct is to stay with the herd. In response, a growing number of sanctuaries now allow tourists to observe elephants without riding them.
Conservation of wild elephants faces other challenges. Although adult elephants have no natural predators, calves can become prey for tigers, and poaching for ivory remains a threat in parts of Asia. As forests shrink, elephants increasingly wander into farms, leading to conflict with villagers. Ironically, the same grey colour that provides camouflage in the forest makes them hard to see at night on rural roads, where accidents with vehicles are rising.
